game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 7, 9, 10, 11.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 7, 7, 8, 10, 10, 11.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The sum's expected value is 9.25 + 53/6 ≈ 18.08, so I'm centering the quotes there. Nothing is revealed yet, so I'm using a fairly wide spread to protect against informed counterparties, with bid 17.5 and ask 18.7.

{"bid": 17.5, "ask": 18.7}

The sum has mean about 18.08 before any information. Quote 1 saw no trade, which is weak evidence that the sum is near the middle, so I put the fair value at roughly 18.05. I'll quote a spread of about 1.3 around that, close to the previous quote.

{"bid": 17.4, "ask": 18.7}

Die 1 is 11, so the sum is 11 plus die 2, which is 18, 19, 21 or 22. Our stage-1 sell at 17.4 was most likely from a noise trader, since an informed seller could not have sold at 17.4 with die 1 = 11. Our position is long, and the posterior on the informed share is about 0.27. Estimated public fair value is about 19.3.

- **Bid 18.0:** Noise sellers are fairly likely below 18. Informed sellers arrive only when the sum is below the bid, and the sum of 18 is not below 18, so nothing is adversely selected here. Expected edge is about +0.26 per unit.
- **Ask 20.9:** Noise buyers come in regularly above 20.9. Informed buyers arrive only when the sum is 21 or 22, which costs a little. This is near the best ask on my rough calculation, with expected edge about +0.17 per unit.

Both sides stay within the ±3 position limit from +1.

{"bid": 18.0, "ask": 20.9}

Die 2 is still hidden, so the public fair value is 11 + E[die 2] = 11 + 53/6 ≈ 19.83. The sum is 18, 19, 21 or 22 with probabilities 1/3, 1/6, 1/3, 1/6. Because this is the last quote of the round, the only question is the expected profit from this one trade. Position is +1 and the position is closed at settlement, so I maximise each side's expected contribution separately.

- **Ask:** an informed buyer takes the ask only if the sum exceeds it, so an ask of 22.0 gets no informed trades. Noise buyers take it with probability about 0.11 × 0.52 ≈ 0.06. Lowering the ask below 22 costs more from informed buys than it gains, so 22.0 is best.
- **Bid:** an informed seller hits the bid only if the sum is below it. A bid of 18.0 avoids informed sells. Noise sellers arrive with probability about 0.15 × 0.52, and raising the bid above 18 starts to draw informed sells, so 18.0 is best.

Expected marginal contribution of this quote is roughly +0.28.

{"bid": 18.0, "ask": 22.0}

Fair value for the sum is about 18.08 (die 1 mean 9.25 plus die 2 mean 8.83). The round 1 trade at 17.4 is weak evidence about alpha, so I'll keep a spread similar to my first quote last round, centred near fair value, to limit adverse selection from informed traders.

{"bid": 17.4, "ask": 18.8}

Round 2 has had no reveal yet, so my fair value starts at 18.08 (6 + 9.25 + 8.83 → E[sum] = 18.08). The 17.4 sale to us is a public trade, and it pulls the posterior mean of the sum down to about 17.6. From the trade history, the chance that the arriving counterparty is informed is roughly 0.2. I'm treating the sum's distribution as discrete, using its 24 equally likely combinations, and maximising expected profit on each side. The bid around 16.0 and ask around 19.3 maximise expected profit from noise and informed trades, given the 1.8 noise standard deviation.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 19.3}

Die 1 is 7, so the settlement is 7 plus die 2. That gives an expected value of about 15.83 (die 2 averages 8.83). Noise traders' willingness to trade depends only on the public fair value, so their trades carry no information about the settlement. Only informed traders create adverse selection.

- **Bid:** Buying at 14.1 has the best expected edge: about 0.15 per unit from noise sellers, with little informed-seller risk since only the 14 outcome falls below the bid.
- **Ask:** Selling at 18.0 has the best expected edge: about 0.12 per unit, since only the 18 outcome sits above the ask to hurt us from informed buyers.

With 2 units long, the position limit allows one more buy before the bid is pulled, and expected profit is roughly the same for either side, so I'm quoting both.

{"bid": 14.1, "ask": 18.0}

Die 2 is still hidden, so the public fair value is 7 + E[die 2] = 7 + 53/6 ≈ 15.83. The settlement can be 14, 15, 17 or 18.

- **Bid at 14.0:** An informed seller only arrives when the value is below my bid. The lowest possible value is 14, so an informed trader never sells to me here. Noise sellers arrive when their valuation is below 14, and buying from them is worth about +1.8 per unit in expectation.
- **Ask at 18.0:** An informed buyer only arrives when the value is above my ask. The highest possible value is 18, so an informed buyer never lifts this ask. Noise buyers arrive when their valuation is above 18, and selling to them is worth about +2.2 per unit. This also reduces my long position of +2.

Both prices are safe whatever the value of alpha, so I don't need to update on the earlier trades.

{"bid": 14.0, "ask": 18.0}

Fair value before any reveal is E[die 1] + E[die 2] = 9.25 + 8.83 ≈ 18.08. The sum's standard deviation is about 2.16. Informed counterparties (expected alpha ≈ 0.48) trade against any quote that sits near the fair value, so the spread needs to be wide. Treating the expected loss to informed flow against the expected profit from noise flow, the break-even distance is about 2.1 on each side. That puts the bid near 16.0 and the ask near 20.2.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 20.2}

Die 1 is 9, so the sum is 9 + die 2, which takes values {16, 16, 17, 19, 19, 20} with equal probability. The fair value is 17.83.

Using the prior mean alpha ≈ 0.48, expected profit per side is roughly:
- **Bid:** Informed sellers arrive only when the sum is below the bid. A bid near 16.8 keeps that adverse-selection loss small while still earning on noise sellers, and bids of 16.9 or higher come out near zero expected profit.
- **Ask:** Informed buyers arrive only when the sum is above the ask. An ask of 20.0 is safe from them, since the sum never exceeds 20, and it earns more from noise buyers than lower asks do.

{"bid": 16.8, "ask": 20.0}

Die 1 = 9 and die 2 is uniform over {7, 7, 8, 10, 10, 11}, so the settlement S is 16, 17, 19, or 20 with probabilities 1/3, 1/6, 1/3, 1/6. The public fair value is 9 + 53/6 ≈ 17.83. Noise traders value the contract at about 17.83 ± 1.8.

Early in the session, a no-trade at ask 18.7 when S was 19 suggests an informed buyer would have hit it. Combined with the other trades, that points to a low alpha, roughly 0.15. Because expected profit is linear in alpha, I used that posterior mean.

Optimizing the expected profit from each side gives:
- **Bid:** about 16.2. Below 16 the marginal noise-seller gain is still positive, and above 16 the informed seller at S = 16 starts to hurt.
- **Ask:** about 19.3. This balances the noise buyers you lose against the informed buyer at S = 20 you still face.

{"bid": 16.2, "ask": 19.3}

Stage 1 has nothing revealed yet, so the fair value is the mean of the sum: E[die 1] = 9.25 and E[die 2] = 8.83, giving 18.08.

The past trades suggest alpha is probably low or middling, not 0.9. In round 1, no trade happened at ask 18.7 even though the settled value was 19, which an informed buyer would have taken. My rough posterior puts the mean alpha near 0.28.

Against noise traders, which sit around 18.08 with sd 1.8, I want quotes wide enough to limit losses to informed traders. I'm treating each side's expected profit as noise-trader edge minus expected informed loss, weighted by mean alpha. On the ask side, 20.0 scores best. On the bid side, 16.3 scores best.

{"bid": 16.3, "ask": 20.0}

**Reasoning**

- **Fair value:** Die 1 averages 9.25 and die 2 averages 8.83, so the public fair value is about 18.08. Die 1 is not yet revealed, so this is the stage-1 fair value.
- **Posterior on alpha:** Past quotes weakly favour low or middling alpha. The no-trade at the 18.7 ask in round 1 is evidence against a high alpha, since an informed buyer would have hit it. Weighting each alpha by the likelihood of the observed trades gives roughly 0.47 for 0.05, 0.51 for 0.5 and 0.02 for 0.9. The posterior mean is about 0.30.
- **Adverse selection:** Informed counterparties buy only when the settlement value exceeds my ask, and sell only when it falls below my bid. Using the exact sum distribution (14 to 22), I maximised expected profit per quote, with noise traders centred at 18.08 with sd 1.8.
  - Ask: about 20.0 is optimal.
  - Bid: about 15.8 to 15.9 is optimal. 15.9 is slightly better than 16.3, the previous bid.

{"bid": 15.9, "ask": 20.0}

Die 2 has expected value 53/6 ≈ 8.83, so the fair value of the sum is 9 + 8.83 ≈ 17.83. Two quotes with no trades this round make a low alpha somewhat more likely, but the posterior mean is still around 0.55. Informed traders can only hit my quotes if the true value (16, 17, 19 or 20) is outside the spread, so I'm keeping the ask at 20.0 (only noise traders can buy there) and moving the bid up slightly from 15.9 to 16.0. Hitting 16.0 requires an informed seller to see V < 16, which never happens.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 20.0}

Die 2 has mean 53/6 ≈ 8.83, so the public fair value of the sum is 9 + 8.83 ≈ 17.83. The possible sums are 16, 17, 19 and 20. Informed counterparties only trade when the sum falls outside my quotes, so they cannot hit a bid of 16 or an ask of 20. Noise traders are centred on 17.83 with SD 1.8, so they buy at 20 about 11% of the time and sell at 16 about 15% of the time.

- **Ask:** Lowering the ask toward 19 would attract more noise buyers, but it would also let informed buyers take the sum-20 outcome at a loss. Since informed traders may be more likely than the prior 1/3 weight suggests (three quiet quotes shift weight toward high α), the informed loss dominates, so 20.0 is best.
- **Bid:** Raising the bid above 16 would let informed sellers take the sum-16 outcome (probability 1/3) at a loss, which outweighs the extra noise flow. Bid 16.0 is best.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 20.0}

**Quote 1 of round 5 (stage 1, nothing revealed)**

- **Fair value:** E[die 1] = 37/4 = 9.25 and E[die 2] = 53/6 ≈ 8.83, so the public fair value is about 18.08.
- **Posterior on alpha:** Round 1 quote 1 got no trade where an informed buyer at 18.7 would have traded against a settlement of 19. That is strong evidence against alpha = 0.9. Round 2 quote 1 (a sale at 17.4 with settlement 17) is consistent with an informed seller. Combining the observations gives roughly P(0.05) ≈ 0.31, P(0.5) ≈ 0.65, P(0.9) ≈ 0.04, so E[alpha] ≈ 0.37.
- **Quote choice:** Since expected profit is linear in alpha, I used E[alpha] ≈ 0.37. For the ask, the trade-off between the noise-trader spread and informed-buyer losses is nearly flat between 20.0 and 20.1, with 20.0 marginally better. For the bid, the best value is at 16.0, with 16.1 and 15.9 slightly worse.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 20.0}

Fair value before any reveal is E[die 1] + E[die 2] = 9.25 + 8.83 ≈ 18.08. Trades so far have been rare, and the history points to a fairly low informed share, so I estimate alpha at roughly 0.37 (posterior mean). Balancing expected noise-trader gains against informed-trader losses at that alpha puts the bid near 16.1 and the ask near 20.0.

{"bid": 16.1, "ask": 20.0}

Die 2 is still hidden, so the public fair value is 11 + E[die 2] = 11 + 53/6 ≈ 19.83.

Informed counterparties buy from my ask only when the settlement is above it, and sell to my bid only when it is below. The possible settlements are 18, 18, 19, 21, 21, 22, so pricing inside the range exposes me to informed trades.

- **Ask at 22:** No settlement exceeds 22, so informed buyers never trade. Only noise buyers can, at about 11% probability with about 2.17 expected edge, giving roughly 0.25 × (1 − α).
- **Ask at 21:** Informed buyers trade on the 22 outcome and lose about 1 each. The expected value is about 0.30(1 − α) − 0.17α, which is worse on average.
- **Bid at 18:** No settlement is below 18, so informed sellers never trade. Noise sellers trade about 15% of the time with about 1.83 edge, giving roughly 0.28 × (1 − α).
- **Bid at 19:** Informed sellers trade on the 18 outcomes and lose about 1 each, which is worse on average.

Quoting 18 and 22 keeps me clear of informed flow on both sides and earns the noise-trader edge.

{"bid": 18, "ask": 22}

Die 2 is still hidden, so the sum is 11 + die 2, which is 18, 19, 21 or 22 with probabilities 1/3, 1/6, 1/3, 1/6. The public fair value is 11 + 53/6 ≈ 19.83.

- **Bid at 18.0:** No informed seller can hit it, since the lowest possible value is 18. Noise sellers arrive with about a 15% chance and give an expected gain of roughly 1.8 per unit.
- **Ask at 22.0:** No informed buyer can lift it, since buying requires value above 22. Noise buyers arrive with about an 11% chance and give an expected gain of roughly 2.2 per unit.

Averaged over the three possible values of alpha, these two prices have the best expected profit of the options I checked. Quoting tighter would expose me to informed flow, and the lack of trades so far in this round is mild evidence that alpha is low.

{"bid": 18.0, "ask": 22.0}

Round 6 starts with nothing revealed, so the public fair value is the mean of the sum: die 1 averages 9.25 and die 2 averages 8.83, giving about 18.08.

The history points to a low informed share. Several quotes at asks of 18.7 to 20 went unhit, which an informed buyer would have taken on values of 19 and 21. So I put alpha near 0.05 to 0.1, with a small chance of 0.5, and use an effective alpha of about 0.12.

With a noise valuation of N(18.08, 1.8²), the expected profit from the ask rises with the distance from fair value, then falls as trades become less likely. Adding the adverse-selection cost from informed buyers, who take the ask only when the sum exceeds it, puts the best ask near 19.6. The bid, which is slightly closer to fair value, lands near 16.6.

{"bid": 16.6, "ask": 19.6}

Public fair value is the expected sum: E[die 1] = 9.25 and E[die 2] = 53/6 ≈ 8.83, so the fair value is about 18.08. Nothing about this round has been revealed yet, so I'm centering on that. Alpha is unknown (average around 0.48), so I'll keep a fairly wide spread of about 3, similar to my first quote this round, to limit losses to informed counterparties. Nothing has traded yet this round, so I'm not adjusting for position.

{"bid": 16.6, "ask": 19.6}

Die 1 is 11, so the sum is 11 + die 2, which takes values 18, 19, 21 or 22. The earlier quotes make alpha probably low (about 0.7 weight on 0.05, 0.25 on 0.5), and the two no-trade quotes in stage 1 tilt die 2 toward its low faces. That puts the public fair value near 19.4, with V = 18 the most likely outcome.

Bid 18.0 is the best bid under this posterior. An informed seller only appears if V < bid, and V = 18 is the lowest possible outcome, so a bid of 18.0 mostly attracts noise sellers at a favourable price.

Ask 21.0 is near the best ask. Noise buyers at 21 pay about 1.5 over fair value, and the informed buyer risk is small because only V = 22 is clearly above 21.

{"bid": 18.0, "ask": 21.0}

Die 2 is uniform on {7, 7, 8, 10, 10, 11}, so the settlement is 11 + die 2, which takes 18, 19, 21 or 22 with probabilities 1/3, 1/6, 1/3, 1/6. The public fair value is about 19.83. The history points to a low alpha, so I use an effective alpha of about 0.25 when weighing adverse selection.

- **Ask:** A sale closes my +1 long at a price above fair value. Noise buyers at 21.5 are unlikely but profitable, and informed buyers only take the ask when settlement is 22, so the expected gain peaks around 21.5.
- **Bid:** Buying a second unit is only worth doing at or below about 18. Above that, informed sellers at settlement 18 erase the edge, so 18.0 is about optimal.

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Four dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, loaded): 3 (prob 1/5), 4 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 2/5), 12 (prob 3/10).
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 10, 11, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 10.
- Die 4 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 1, 2, 9, 10.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** Die 2 is not yet revealed, so the expected sum is the sum of the expected faces:
- Die 1: 7.0
- Die 2: 61/8 = 7.625
- Die 3: 22/6 ≈ 3.67
- Die 4: 22/6 ≈ 3.67

Fair value ≈ 21.96. Settlement uncertainty is about 7.1 (standard deviation), mostly from the unrevealed dice.

**Spread:** Alpha is unknown (0.05, 0.5, or 0.9, equally likely). Against noise traders (sd 6), tight quotes earn more flow. Against informed traders, tight quotes are picked off. Averaging expected profit per side over the three alpha values, a half-spread of about 8 maximizes it. Stage 2 can be tighter, since die 2 will be revealed by then.

Quotes: bid ≈ 21.96 − 8 = 13.96, rounded down to 13.9; ask ≈ 29.96, rounded up to 30.0.

{"bid": 13.9, "ask": 30.0}

**Estimate of the settlement value.** Die 2 = 10 is revealed. The expected values of the hidden dice are: die 1 = 7.0, die 3 = 22/6 ≈ 3.67, die 4 = 22/6 ≈ 3.67. So the public fair value is about 10 + 7 + 3.67 + 3.67 ≈ 24.3.

**Update on alpha.** The quote-2 sale at 13.9 cannot come from an informed trader, since the settlement value is at least 14 (10 + 3 + 1 + 0). So it was a noise trader, which is weak evidence that alpha is low. Combining that with the no-trade result at quotes 1 and 2, my posterior mean for alpha is about 0.26.

**Choosing the quotes.** I compared the expected per-quote profit at different prices, weighting noise traders (valuation about 24.3 ± 6) and informed traders (who trade only when the settlement value is past my quote):
- Ask: 28 gives about 0.45, 29 about 0.51, 30 about 0.53, 31 about 0.51. The informed buyers' right tail (die 1 = 12) makes the ask side costly, so 30 is about optimal.
- Bid: 18.5 gives about 0.62, with 18 and 19 close behind. Informed sellers are rarer below the bid, since the settlement value rarely falls that low.

These are one-quote estimates, and I ignored the small downward shift in fair value from the no-trade results. My position is +1, so a bid of 18.5 keeps me inside the limit.

**Fair value:** Die 2 is known to be 10. The expected values of the unrevealed dice are:
- Die 1: 3(0.2) + 4(0.1) + 6(0.4) + 12(0.3) = 7.0
- Die 3: 22/6 ≈ 3.67
- Die 4: 22/6 ≈ 3.67

So the public fair value is about 24.33. The settlement's standard deviation is about 6.2, and the sum ranges from 14 to 42.

**Inferring alpha:** The sale at 13.9 cannot have come from an informed trader, because the settlement is at least 14. It was a noise trader, which makes low alpha more likely. The other quotes were roughly uninformative. My posterior is about 0.61 on alpha = 0.05, 0.32 on 0.5, and 0.06 on 0.9, for an expected alpha of about 0.24.

**Quote:** Noise traders arrive around 24.33 with standard deviation 6. Informed traders take the side that is wrong for me. Optimising the expected profit at the expected alpha gives a half-spread of about 0.9 standard deviations, roughly 5.4. That puts the bid near 18.9 and the ask near 29.7, rounded to 18.9 and 29.8. My position of +1 does not change this, since the position is marked at its expected settlement value.

Expected settlement given public info: die 1 has mean 7.0, die 2 has mean 7.625, and dice 3 and 4 each have mean about 3.67. game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 5 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The public fair value of the settlement (heads in 5 flips) is 1.75, since E[p] = 0.35. Because alpha's prior mean is about 0.48, informed traders are a large share of flow. Quoting near fair value would lose money: an ask at 2.0 has expected profit of roughly -0.14 per quote, and a bid at 1.5 is similarly negative. Prices far from the fair value earn at best about zero, so I'm quoting a low bid only, where noise sellers are a small edge and informed sellers can't profitably hit me, and leaving the ask effectively out of the money.

{"bid": 0.1, "ask": 5.0}

With no flips revealed yet, the fair value is 5 × (0.5×0.2 + 0.5×0.5) = 1.75. Informed counterparties know the settlement count K, so they trade against me whenever my quote is mispriced relative to K.

- **Ask:** Expected profit from a sale is negative at every price I checked below 5. Noise buyers rarely reach high asks, and informed buyers take the asks that are below K. An ask of 5 is effectively no quote, so I'll keep it there for a near-zero expected result.
- **Bid:** Expected profit from a purchase at bid b is roughly 0.517·P(V<b)·(1.75−b) + 0.483·E[(K−b)·1{K<b}]. At b = 0 an informed seller can never trade, since K ≥ 0, so every fill is non-negative. The expected value is about +0.02, which beats b = 0.1 (about +0.017) and b = 0.2 (about +0.014).

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 5.0}

Fair value before any flips are revealed is 1.75. Settlement is the number of heads in 5 flips from a coin that is 0.2 or 0.5 with equal odds, so the mean is 5 × 0.35 = 1.75. Round 1 had no trades, which gives little evidence about whether alpha is high or low, so I use the prior mean alpha ≈ 0.48.

Settlement is an integer and noise traders' valuations have only 0.88 standard deviation around 1.75. An informed trader trades against any quote near fair value, and that adverse selection outweighs the noise flow. Checking candidate quotes with expected profit per quote:

- Ask 2.5 to 3.0: negative, about -0.005 to -0.05.
- Ask 5.0: about 0, since no informed trader buys (settlement can't exceed 5).
- Bid 0.0: about +0.02, since informed traders never sell here and noise traders occasionally sell below 0.
- Bids from 0.1 to 0.9 earn less, and bids at 0.7 and above turn negative.

So I quote bid 0 and ask 5.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 5}

Before any flips are revealed, the fair value is E[heads] = 5 × (0.2 + 0.5)/2 = 1.75.

Informed counterparties (who know the settlement value V) trade against me whenever my quote is stale relative to V, so I want quotes that only trade when the expected gain outweighs that risk. Averaging over the prior on alpha (mean ≈ 0.48), I checked the expected per-quote profit on each side:

- **Ask:** Asks near fair value lose money on net, because informed buyers hit them whenever V is high. An ask of 5 is effectively a pass, and asks around 4 are slightly negative.
- **Bid:** A bid of 0 is never hit by informed sellers, since V cannot be below 0. It only trades with noise sellers whose valuation falls below 0 (about 2% of the time), giving a small positive expected profit. Higher bids (0.1 to 0.6) are less profitable because informed sellers start to trade against them.

I'll keep this wide quote and reassess once flips 1 to 3 are revealed before stage 2.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 5}

**Public fair value:** Flips 1-3 were all tails, so the settlement is the number of heads in flips 4 and 5, which is 0, 1, or 2. The posterior on the fair coin (p=0.2 with probability about 0.80) gives a fair value of about 0.52.

**Bid:** A bid of 0 is safe. Informed traders sell to me only when the settlement is below my bid, which is impossible at 0. Noise traders sell to me below 0 about 28% of the time, with an expected profit of about 0.5 per unit.

**Ask:** Informed traders buy from me only when the settlement exceeds my ask. A 1.5 ask is exceeded only when the settlement is 2 (about 8% chance), so the adverse selection is small. Noise traders buy from me about 13% of the time at that price. Averaging over the three possible values of alpha, an ask around 1.4 to 1.5 has the highest expected profit, so I'm using 1.5. A higher alpha would argue for a wider ask, but the difference is small.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.5}

**Reasoning:** Flips 1-3 were all tails, so the coin is probably the 0.2 coin (posterior about 0.80). The expected settlement is about 0.52 (two unrevealed flips). Informed counterparties can only sell to me if S < bid, or buy if S > ask. Noise traders have valuation near 0.52 with SD 0.88. The round-2 trade at bid 0 was a noise seller, which points toward a low alpha.

- **Bid 0:** Informed traders never sell here, since S ≥ 0. Noise sellers at 0 give me a unit worth about 0.52 on average, so this is positive expected value. Higher bids add adverse selection from informed sellers when S = 0.
- **Ask 1.2:** I'm already long 1. Selling at 1.2 has expected value of about +0.087 per quote, which beats the alternatives I checked (1.0 ≈ 0.076, 1.5 ≈ 0.080, 2.0 ≈ 0.049). Informed buyers only take it when S = 2.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.2}

Public fair value is 1.75 (5 flips × E[p] = 5 × 0.35), and nothing is revealed yet this round. Noise-trader sales at my bid and purchases at my ask are unbiased relative to fair value, but informed traders adversely select against me. Averaging over alpha ∈ {0.05, 0.5, 0.9} with equal weight:

- **Bid:** A bid of 0 is the best option. Informed sellers can't appear at 0, since V ≥ 0 and they only sell when V < bid. Noise sellers arrive with probability about 2.3%, at about 1.75 of edge each, giving an expected profit of about +0.02 per quote. Raising the bid adds informed adverse selection faster than noise flow.
- **Ask:** Asks around 2.5–3.5 are negative on average, because the informed buyers at high alpha outweigh the gains at low alpha. An ask of 5 is essentially break-even (V ≤ 5, so informed buyers never arrive), and it's marginally better than 4 on average.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 5}

Revealed flips 1 to 3 are all tails, so the coin is probably the 0.2 coin. The posterior is about 0.80 for p=0.2 and 0.20 for p=0.5. That puts the expected settlement near 0.52, which is the public fair value for noise traders.

- **Bid at 0:** Informed traders would only sell to me if the settlement were below 0, which is impossible, so only noise sellers can hit this bid. Those sellers value the contract below 0, while fair value is about 0.52, so each trade has positive expected profit.
- **Ask at 1.3:** Informed buyers can only take this ask when the settlement is 2, and noise buyers come in when their valuation exceeds 1.3. Averaging over alpha, I estimate the expected profit from the ask is highest around 1.2 to 1.3, with 1.3 slightly better. This is a rough estimate and the alpha-averaged calculation is approximate.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.3}

The last flips were tails, so the posterior on the fair coin is about 80% p=0.2 and 20% p=0.5. The expected settlement is about 0.52, which gives a fair value near 0.52. Flips 4 and 5 are the only unknowns, so the settlement S is 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities of roughly 0.56, 0.36 and 0.08.

Pricing each side against noise traders and informed traders, averaging over alpha (mean 0.48):
- **Ask:** about 1.3 to 1.4 maximises expected profit (about 0.05 per quote). Pricing at 1.0 or below loses money to informed buyers.
- **Bid:** 0.1 is the only useful bid level (about 0.04 per quote). A bid of 0 cannot be hit by anyone.

Quoting both sides gives at most one trade, and the position closes at settlement, so the expected inventory cost is zero.

{"bid": 0.1, "ask": 1.4}

Before any flips are revealed, the expected number of heads is 5 × (0.2 + 0.5)/2 = 1.75. The settlement distribution is wide (roughly 18% at 0, 28% at 1, 26% at 2, 18% at 3, 8% at 4, 2% at 5), so informed counterparties would trade against a tight quote. Past quotes give little evidence about alpha. With alpha uncertain, a wide two-sided quote near 1.75 roughly breaks even in expectation and limits adverse selection if alpha is 0.9. I'll tighten in stage 2, once flips 1–3 are revealed.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 3.0}

**Posterior after the trade:** Nothing is revealed yet, so the public prior mean is 1.75. A counterparty selling to us at 0.5 is most likely informed with a settlement of 0. That gives P(settlement = 0 | trade) ≈ 0.74 and a public fair value of about 0.55.

**Bid:** Any bid above 0 is likely to be hit by an informed seller when the settlement is 0, which costs us the bid. A bid of 0 avoids this and still earns from noise sellers, so I quote 0.

**Ask:** The informed-buyer risk is smaller on the ask side, because informed buyers need a settlement above the ask. Expected profit from an ask around 1.5 is slightly positive, and it is the best of the values I checked (1.3 to 1.6).

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.5}

**Posterior:** Flips 1–3 were all tails, so the settlement is S = flip 4 + flip 5, which can be 0, 1 or 2. The coin posterior is P(p=0.2) ≈ 0.80 and P(p=0.5) ≈ 0.20. That gives a public fair value of about 0.52, with P(S=0) ≈ 0.56, P(S=1) ≈ 0.36 and P(S=2) ≈ 0.08.

**Ask:** You are long 1, so selling above fair value is the main edge. Against noise traders, the expected gain peaks near fair value plus about 0.66, which is roughly 1.18. Informed buyers only take the ask when S = 2, which adds a small adverse cost. Asks near 1.2 maximize the expected value.

**Bid:** Noise traders sell to you at prices below fair value. The best noise-only bid would be slightly negative, so I use 0. An informed seller never trades at 0 because S ≥ 0, so there is no adverse selection on this side.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.2}

**Posterior after three tails:** P(coin has bias 0.2) = 0.512 / (0.512 + 0.125) ≈ 0.80. The expected number of heads in flips 4 and 5 is about 0.52, so the public fair value is about 0.52.

**Settlement distribution given the posterior:** P(S=0) ≈ 0.56, P(S=1) ≈ 0.36, P(S=2) ≈ 0.08.

**Bid:** An informed seller hits a bid of 0 only if S < 0, which never happens, so a bid of 0 faces no adverse selection. Noise traders with valuation below 0 (probability about 0.28) sell to us at a profit of roughly 0.52 each. A bid of 0.1 or higher loses to informed sellers when S = 0 and earns less from noise sellers, so 0 is the best bid.

**Ask:** An ask near 1.4 avoids informed buyers, who only buy when S ≥ 2 (probability about 0.08), while still attracting noise buyers whose valuation exceeds 1.4 (probability about 0.16). Averaged over the three possible values of alpha, this comes out slightly ahead of asks at 1.3 or 1.5, and well ahead of asks below 1.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 1.4}

Nothing is revealed yet, so the public fair value is the prior mean: 5 × (0.5×0.2 + 0.5×0.5) = 1.75. I'm quoting a wide, roughly symmetric market around it. Adverse selection from informed traders (who know the settlement) is the main cost, and a spread of about 0.5 to 3.0 roughly breaks even on expected profit across the three possible alpha values. Stage 2 will reveal three flips, which should let me tighten.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 3.0}

Round 5 stage 2 has revealed flips 1, 2, 3 = 1, 0, 0, so the settlement is S = 1 + X4 + X5. Given the posterior on the coin, the expected settlement is about 1.70, with P(S=1) ≈ 0.45, P(S=2) ≈ 0.41, P(S=3) ≈ 0.14.

Past trades suggest the informed share is moderate, with a posterior mean around 0.36. Informed counterparties sell to a bid only when S is below it, and buy from an ask only when S is above it.

- **Bid 1.0:** S can never be below 1, so informed sellers are excluded. Noise sellers arrive with probability about 0.21, each giving an expected profit of about 0.70. This is near the best bid, since higher bids add adverse selection faster than noise flow.
- **Ask 2.6:** Only S = 3 can make an informed buyer trade, and that costs about 0.4 per trade. Noise buyers arrive with probability about 0.16, each giving about 0.90. This is the best ask in the model, better than 3.0, which attracts few trades.

This is a rough single-quote model, not a full dynamic solution.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 2.6}

Fair value is about 1.70. Flip 1 was heads, and flips 2 and 3 were tails, so the posterior on the coin is roughly even (about 51% biased). That puts the expected heads in flips 4 and 5 near 0.70. The settlement is 1 + (heads in flips 4 and 5), so it is 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities of about 0.45, 0.41 and 0.14.

- **Bid 1.0:** Noise sellers arrive when their valuation is below 1.0, about 21% of the time, earning roughly 0.7 each. Informed sellers only sell when the settlement is below 1.0, which cannot happen, so they add no adverse selection.
- **Ask 2.5:** Noise buyers come in about 18% of the time, earning roughly 0.8 each. Informed buyers only buy when the settlement is 3, which is worth 0.5 against the ask. This gives the best expected result across the three possible values of alpha.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 2.5}

The fair value is 1.75: the coin's bias is 0.2 or 0.5 with equal probability, so the expected heads over 5 flips is 5 × 0.35. Nothing is revealed yet this round.

- **Bid at 0:** An informed seller would only sell if the settlement value were below 0, which can't happen, so only noise traders can hit this bid. Their valuation falls below 0 about 2% of the time, and each such trade earns roughly 1.75 in expectation. Averaged over the alpha prior, this is slightly positive.
- **Ask:** Informed buyers take any ask below the settlement value, so a low ask gives away value to them. Expected profit is about zero near 3 and slightly negative below that. A high ask such as 4.5 is almost never hit and is essentially neutral, so I'm quoting it there to avoid adverse selection before the stage 2 information arrives.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4.5}

The public fair value is 1.75: the coin's bias averages 0.35, so 5 flips give 1.75 heads on average. Nothing is revealed yet, so this is the prior.

Against that baseline, I weighed informed-trader adverse selection (buying at my ask when the settlement is high, selling at my bid when it is low) against noise-trader flow, which only trades when its valuation (normal, mean 1.75, sd 0.88) is far from fair value. With alpha averaging about 0.48:

- **Bid:** Bids around 0.1 to 0.2 earn a small positive expected edge, mainly from noise sellers. A bid of 0.1 is about as good as 0.

{"bid": 0.1, "ask": 4.0}

- **Bid:** Selling to me at 3.0 can only come from noise traders, since an informed trader sells only when the settlement is below my bid and that can't happen at 3.0. - **Ask:** At 5.0 an informed trader never buys, because settlement cannot exceed 5. The only trades are noise buyers with valuation above 5, and the expected profit from them is about 0.12 per unit. Averaging over alpha (each of 0.05, 0.5, 0.9 with probability 1/3), the best pair is bid 3.0 and ask 5.0.

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 3, 10.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 5, 7, 10, 11, 11.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Before any reveal, the fair value is the expected max of the three dice. Working through P(max > x) for each integer threshold gives E[max] ≈ 9.45. Nothing has been revealed, so I'm centering on that. The previous ask of 11.5 drew no buyer, which is mild evidence against a very high value. I'm quoting a symmetric spread of roughly ±1 around 9.45 to cover adverse selection from informed flow, since alpha is unknown.

{"bid": 8.4, "ask": 10.5}

**Settlement value:** With die 3 = 7, the settlement is max(7, d1, d2). P(M=7) = 3/8, P(M=10) = 7/24, P(M=11) = 1/3, so E[S] ≈ 9.21.

**Bid:** Informed sellers hit my bid only when S < B. At bids above 7, they hit it when S = 7, which loses money on average. A bid of 7.0 avoids that, since S = 7 is not strictly below 7. It still catches noise sellers with valuations below 7 (about 11%), who are worth about 2.2 each to me. Among the candidate bids, 7.0 gives the best expected value.

**Ask:** Informed buyers take my ask only when S > A. At 11.0 they never do, because S can't exceed 11 once die 3 = 7. game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.
